exam_name: ISTQB Certified Tester Testing with Generative AI

questions.question: A team's RAG chatbot answers correctly for single-fact questions but garbles answers requiring arithmetic over retrieved numbers, such as summing values from a table. What is the most likely explanation?

options.D: LLMs are not reliable calculators
options.A: The retrieval step is broken and must be fixed first
options.B: The context window is too large
options.C: Temperature is set too high and must be lowered to zero

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: lLMs are not reliable calculators; multi-step numeric reasoning over retrieved data needs a tool such as a calculator or code execution rather than pure generation.

questions.question: A support bot's tone shifts from formal to casual mid-conversation with no user request to change it. What GenAI foundation concept explains the likely cause and fix?

options.B: Instruction adherence can drift over a long conversation as earlier system guidance loses relative weight
options.A: The model's vocabulary size changed during the conversation, though this is not accurate
options.C: The vector database ran out of storage, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: The user's IP address changed, resetting the model's persona, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: instruction adherence can drift over a long conversation as earlier system guidance loses relative weight; re-asserting key instructions periodically in context helps.

questions.question: A team wants to add a calendar-booking capability to their assistant. Which architecture choice is most appropriate and why?

options.D: Give the model a tool or function it can call to check and book calendar slots
options.A: Fine-tune the base model on the company's entire calendar history, which does not hold here
options.B: Increase the temperature so the model is more willing to take action, which testers often assume
options.C: Rely on the model to describe the booking in text and have a human retype it every time

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: give the model a tool or function it can call to check and book calendar slots, since arbitrary real-world side effects should not be produced by free-form generation.

questions.question: An assistant built on RAG cites the wrong document version after the knowledge base was updated. What foundational gap does this most likely reveal?

options.C: The retrieval index was not refreshed or re-embedded after the source documents changed
options.A: The model's context window shrank after the update, though it misses the actual cause
options.B: The system prompt is missing a greeting, as some teams mistakenly believe
options.D: The temperature was set to zero at the wrong time, which confuses two separate concepts

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: the retrieval index was not refreshed or re-embedded after the source documents changed, so stale embeddings point to outdated content.

questions.question: A tester is asked whether a fine-tuned model or a RAG-based approach is better for a policy document assistant that changes weekly. Which is the stronger recommendation and why?

options.D: RAG, because updating the retrieved document set is far faster and cheaper than retraining a model every time the policy changes
options.A: Fine-tuning, because retrained models never need any further testing, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: Neither; only prompt engineering should ever be used, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.C: RAG, because it eliminates the need for any evaluation, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: rAG, because updating the retrieved document set is far faster and cheaper than retraining a model every time the policy changes.

questions.question: An agent occasionally calls a tool with a malformed argument, such as a string where a number is expected, and the tool call fails silently. Which foundational concept should guide the fix?

options.D: Tool and function-calling interfaces need schema validation and clear error feedback to the model so it can retry or report the failure correctly
options.A: The model's embedding dimension needs to be increased, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.B: The issue can only be fixed by lowering the temperature to zero, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.C: Tool calls never need validation because models always produce well-formed arguments, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: tool and function-calling interfaces need schema validation and clear error feedback to the model so it can retry or report the failure correctly.

questions.question: A team observes that a smaller, cheaper model performs almost as well as a larger one on their specific narrow task after fine-tuning. What foundational principle explains this?

options.B: Task-specific fine-tuning can let a smaller model match a larger general-purpose model's performance on a narrow domain, at lower inference cost
options.A: Smaller models always outperform larger models on every task, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.C: Fine-tuning has no effect on task performance, though closer inspection of the system's behaviour shows this is not the case
options.D: Model size never affects inference cost, an idea that sounds credible in isolation but does not match the documented behaviour of these systems

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: task-specific fine-tuning can let a smaller model match a larger general-purpose model's performance on a narrow domain, at lower inference cost.

questions.question: A chatbot answers "I don't know" far more often after a prompt-template change, even for questions it previously answered correctly. What is the most likely foundational cause to investigate first?

options.C: The prompt template change may have altered how the retrieved context or instructions are presented, unintentionally encouraging abstention
options.A: The model's training data was deleted, though closer inspection of the system's behaviour shows this is not the case
options.B: The vector database's embedding dimension changed on its own, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.D: The user's browser cache needs to be cleared, which reflects a common but mistaken shortcut rather than the specific mechanism actually responsible here

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: the prompt template change may have altered how the retrieved context or instructions are presented, unintentionally encouraging abstention.

questions.question: A team debates whether to increase the number of few-shot examples in a classification prompt from 2 to 10. What foundational trade-off should inform the decision?

options.B: More examples can improve accuracy but increase token cost and latency, and may hit context-window limits
options.A: More examples always reduce token cost, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.C: Few-shot examples have no effect on classification accuracy, which testers often assume
options.D: Adding examples always violates the model's licence terms, based on a common misconception

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: more examples can improve accuracy but increase token cost and latency, and may hit context-window limits, so the benefit must be weighed against those costs.

questions.question: An agent designed to answer HR questions is given access to a broad set of internal tools "just in case" future features need them. Which foundational risk does this create?

options.A: Excess tool access increases the chance of unintended, unsafe, or unauthorised actions if the model misuses a tool it did not actually need for the task
options.B: More tools always make the agent faster, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.C: Tool access has no bearing on safety, only on features, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.D: Extra tools reduce the model's context window automatically, a plausible-sounding shortcut that skips over the deeper technical reason the situation actually occurred

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: excess tool access increases the chance of unintended, unsafe, or unauthorised actions if the model misuses a tool it did not actually need for the task.

questions.question: A team switches their RAG generator from one LLM provider to another and answer quality drops noticeably, even though retrieval is unchanged. What should be investigated first?

options.A: Whether the prompt template, instructions, and context-formatting are well suited to the new model
options.B: Whether the vector database needs to be physically relocated, though it misses the actual cause
options.C: Whether the office network bandwidth has decreased, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.D: Whether the new provider uses a different currency for billing, which does not hold here

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: whether the prompt template, instructions, and context-formatting are well suited to the new model, since prompt effectiveness is often model-specific.

questions.question: A legal-summary assistant is faithful and concise, but a review finds it omits the losing party's argument in half of case summaries. Which quality gap and test fix apply?

options.C: Completeness and coverage of required content
options.A: Latency; measure response time only
options.B: Privacy; scan for personal data, which testers often assume
options.D: Style; check punctuation only, which does not hold here

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: completeness and coverage of required content; add a checklist of must-include elements, such as both parties' arguments, and score against it per case.

questions.question: A translation feature scores well on BLEU but native speakers say the output "sounds unnatural." What additional evaluation should be added?

options.B: Human fluency and naturalness rating on a representative sample
options.A: Increase the temperature to improve BLEU further, which does not hold here
options.C: Remove BLEU entirely and use only automated checks, though this is not accurate
options.D: Reduce the number of translated languages tested, which testers often assume

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: human fluency and naturalness rating on a representative sample, since n-gram overlap does not capture how natural phrasing sounds to native speakers.

questions.question: A code-review assistant flags valid code as buggy about 20% of the time. How should this be classified and measured?

options.B: A false-positive and precision problem
options.A: A latency problem; measure only response time
options.C: A licensing problem; check the code's open-source licence
options.D: Not a defect, since flagging extra issues is always safer

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: a false-positive and precision problem; measure precision of flagged issues against a labelled set of genuinely buggy and genuinely valid code.

questions.question: An assistant answering health questions gives medically accurate information but never recommends seeing a professional when appropriate. What quality gap is this and how should it be tested?

options.C: A safety and appropriateness gap in escalation behaviour
options.A: A latency gap; measure only response speed, which does not hold here
options.B: A privacy gap; scan for PII only, which testers often assume
options.D: Not a defect, since the information given is accurate

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: a safety and appropriateness gap in escalation behaviour; test with scenarios that should trigger a consult-a-professional recommendation and assert it appears.

questions.question: A customer-service bot is graded highly on tone and grammar but resolves only 40% of issues without escalation. Which quality dimension is being under-weighted in the current evaluation?

options.B: Task success and resolution rate, which should be weighted at least as heavily as style
options.A: Font consistency across responses, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: The number of emojis used, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: The length of the greeting message, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: task success and resolution rate, which should be weighted at least as heavily as style, since resolving the user's actual problem is the core value.

questions.question: An image-captioning model is fluent and grammatically correct but frequently describes objects that are not present in the image. What is this failure mode and how is it tested?

options.B: Visual hallucination and grounding failure
options.A: A latency failure; measure image upload speed
options.C: A licensing failure; check the image file format
options.D: Not testable, since captioning is inherently subjective

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: visual hallucination and grounding failure; test by comparing captions against ground-truth object lists for a labelled image set.

questions.question: A GenAI assistant for internal use passes all functional tests but a security review finds it will describe how to bypass the company's own access controls if asked indirectly. Which quality attribute failed and what test category catches it?

options.D: Safety and guardrail robustness
options.A: Latency; only load testing would catch this
options.B: Style adherence; only tone testing would catch this
options.C: Cost efficiency; only token-usage testing would catch this

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: safety and guardrail robustness; adversarial and indirect-request red-team testing targeting the specific restricted topic.

questions.question: A writing assistant consistently produces grammatically perfect text that subtly changes the factual meaning of the user's input when "improving" it. How should this be classified?

options.D: A faithfulness and meaning-preservation defect
options.A: A style defect only, safe to deprioritise
options.B: A latency defect, since rewriting takes time
options.C: A licensing defect, since rewriting changes ownership of text

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: a faithfulness and meaning-preservation defect; measure with a semantic-equivalence check between input and rewritten output on a labelled set.

questions.question: A voice assistant's transcription-plus-response pipeline performs well in quiet-room tests but poorly with background noise in real use. What testing gap does this reveal?

options.C: The test environment did not represent real acoustic conditions
options.A: The model's temperature setting caused the issue, which does not hold here
options.B: The issue can only be in the text-generation stage, not audio input
options.D: Background noise is not a testable condition, which testers often assume

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: the test environment did not represent real acoustic conditions; noisy-audio test cases are needed to evaluate robustness under realistic conditions.

questions.question: A GenAI assistant answering coding questions gives correct code but insecure code, such as SQL built by string concatenation. Which quality dimension is missing from the current test suite?

options.B: Secure-coding correctness
options.A: Latency; only response time matters for code assistants
options.C: Diversity; only output variety matters here
options.D: Not a defect, since the code runs correctly

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: secure-coding correctness; add tests that check generated code against known insecure-pattern rules, not just functional correctness.

questions.question: A product team wants to know if a new prompt reduces hallucinations without hurting helpfulness. Which evaluation design correctly tests both at once?

options.A: Score the same output set on both a faithfulness and hallucination metric and a helpfulness rubric, and compare both dimensions together rather than optimising one in isolation
options.B: Only measure hallucination rate, since helpfulness cannot regress from prompt changes, which reflects a common but mistaken shortcut rather than the specific mechanism actually responsible here
options.C: Only measure helpfulness, since hallucination rate never changes with prompts, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Alternate measuring one dimension per week, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: score the same output set on both a faithfulness and hallucination metric and a helpfulness rubric, and compare both dimensions together rather than optimising one in isolation.

questions.question: An assistant that drafts marketing copy is found to make exaggerated, unverifiable claims about a product's performance. Which quality attribute should be added to its evaluation and how?

options.A: Claim verifiability and factual support
options.B: Font size consistency, which does not hold here
options.C: Number of exclamation marks used
options.D: Only latency, since copy generation should just be fast

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: claim verifiability and factual support; check that performance claims in the copy are supported by approved product facts, flagging unsupported claims.

questions.question: A customer support assistant answers correctly in English but gives noticeably lower-quality answers in Spanish for the same underlying questions. What should the quality report show?

options.C: Per-language quality metrics
options.A: A single combined score across all languages is sufficient
options.B: Spanish support should simply be disabled rather than measured
options.D: Language has no bearing on GenAI output quality

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: per-language quality metrics, since aggregate scores can hide a real disparity that affects Spanish-speaking users specifically.

questions.question: A tester needs to verify a summarisation feature stays within a required word-count range across many varied source documents. Which test design fits best?

options.A: Property-based tests that check word count is within the specified range for every generated summary across a large varied input set
options.B: A single test with one fixed document, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.C: A test that only checks the summary is non-empty, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: A manual review of one summary per quarter, which is the sort of surface-level guess that does not withstand a careful technical review of the case

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: property-based tests that check word count is within the specified range for every generated summary across a large varied input set.

questions.question: A tester wants to confirm a chatbot correctly declines requests for medical dosing advice, including when the request is hidden inside a hypothetical story. Which test design addresses this most directly?

options.D: A red-team test set including direct, indirect, and role-play or hypothetical framings of the restricted request, asserting a safe refusal each time
options.A: A single direct-request test case, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.B: A test that only checks response length, which is the sort of surface-level guess that does not withstand a careful technical review of the case
options.C: A test using only benign, unrelated questions, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: a red-team test set including direct, indirect, and role-play or hypothetical framings of the restricted request, asserting a safe refusal each time.

questions.question: An agent must never exceed a budget of 5 tool calls per task. Which test verifies this reliably?

options.A: Tasks deliberately designed to tempt excessive tool use, asserting the tool-call count stays within budget and the agent still completes or safely aborts
options.B: A single task requiring exactly one tool call, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.C: A test that only checks the agent's final answer text, which might seem reasonable on the surface but is contradicted by how these systems are actually built and tested
options.D: A test that disables tool-call counting to save time, which is the sort of surface-level guess that does not withstand a careful technical review of the case

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: tasks deliberately designed to tempt excessive tool use, asserting the tool-call count stays within budget and the agent still completes or safely aborts.

questions.question: A tester is verifying that rephrasing a factual question gives consistent answers. What kind of test is this?

options.C: A metamorphic and paraphrase-consistency test, checking the substantive answer is stable across meaning-preserving rewordings
options.A: A load test, checking how many requests per second the system handles, which confuses two separate concepts
options.B: A latency test, checking response time only, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: A licensing test, checking data usage rights, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: a metamorphic and paraphrase-consistency test, checking the substantive answer is stable across meaning-preserving rewordings.

questions.question: A tester designs cases where a RAG assistant's retrieved documents are deliberately made empty or irrelevant. What is the correct expected behaviour to assert?

options.A: The assistant should indicate it lacks sufficient information rather than fabricating an answer
options.B: The assistant should always still attempt a confident answer, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: The assistant should crash with an error message, as some teams mistakenly believe
options.D: The assistant should ignore the user's question entirely, though it misses the actual cause

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: the assistant should indicate it lacks sufficient information rather than fabricating an answer.

questions.question: A team wants a stable pass or fail gate for a task where correct answers vary in wording but must contain specific required facts. What is the best assertion design?

options.D: Extract and check for presence of the required facts via keyword or entailment checks
options.A: Assert the answer matches one fixed reference string exactly, which does not hold here
options.B: Assert the answer is under 10 words, though it misses the actual cause
options.C: Assert the answer contains no punctuation, which confuses two separate concepts

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: extract and check for presence of the required facts via keyword or entailment checks, rather than requiring exact wording.

questions.question: A tester wants to check whether a GenAI feature handles a sudden switch of language mid-conversation. Which test design addresses this?

options.A: Multi-turn test cases where the user switches languages partway through, asserting the assistant follows the language switch appropriately
options.B: A single-turn test in one language only, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.C: A test that disables language detection, which reflects a common but mistaken shortcut rather than the specific mechanism actually responsible here
options.D: A test that only measures response latency, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: multi-turn test cases where the user switches languages partway through, asserting the assistant follows the language switch appropriately.

questions.question: An assistant is supposed to refuse to reveal its system prompt. A tester tries ten different phrasings to extract it and nine succeed in getting a refusal, one leaks part of the prompt. What should the test report conclude?

options.D: The refusal behaviour is not sufficiently robust
options.A: A 90% refusal rate is an acceptable pass for this security property
options.B: The test should be discarded because results were inconsistent
options.C: Only the exact phrasing that leaked needs to ever be blocked, nothing broader

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: the refusal behaviour is not sufficiently robust; the leaking phrasing is a real defect requiring investigation, not a statistical fluke to ignore.

questions.question: A tester is verifying an agent correctly recovers when a tool call returns an error, such as "service unavailable." What test design covers this?

options.C: Inject simulated tool-call failures and assert the agent retries appropriately, reports the failure clearly, or falls back safely
options.A: Only test the happy path where every tool call succeeds, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.B: Assert the agent immediately stops responding after any tool error, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Assert the agent ignores tool errors silently, which is the sort of surface-level guess that does not withstand a careful technical review of the case

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: inject simulated tool-call failures and assert the agent retries appropriately, reports the failure clearly, or falls back safely, rather than stalling or fabricating a result.

questions.question: Which test is most appropriate to check that a content-moderation guardrail is not simply keyword-matching a blocklist?

options.D: Test with paraphrases, synonyms, and obfuscated spellings of disallowed content that avoid the literal blocked keywords, and assert the guardrail still catches the intent
options.A: Test only with the exact blocked keywords, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.B: Test only with completely unrelated benign content, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.C: Test with the guardrail disabled, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: test with paraphrases, synonyms, and obfuscated spellings of disallowed content that avoid the literal blocked keywords, and assert the guardrail still catches the intent.

questions.question: A tester wants to check that a summarisation feature's output length scales sensibly with input length, so a one-paragraph input should not produce a ten-page summary. What test design fits?

options.B: A property-based and metamorphic test asserting output length stays within a reasonable proportion of input length across varied input sizes
options.A: A test asserting output length is always exactly 100 words, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.C: A test that only checks spelling, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.D: A test that ignores input length entirely, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: a property-based and metamorphic test asserting output length stays within a reasonable proportion of input length across varied input sizes.

questions.question: A team wants to know whether their guardrail against generating malware code also catches requests phrased as "for educational purposes only." Which test design is correct?

options.D: Include variants of the malicious request with common social-engineering framings, such as educational, fictional, or research, in the red-team suite, asserting refusal in each
options.A: Trust that the framing makes the request safe and skip testing it, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.B: Only test the request with no framing at all, which reflects a common but mistaken shortcut rather than the specific mechanism actually responsible here
options.C: Remove the request from testing since it is edge-case and rare, which is the sort of surface-level guess that does not withstand a careful technical review of the case

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: include variants of the malicious request with common social-engineering framings, such as educational, fictional, or research, in the red-team suite, asserting refusal in each.

questions.question: An assistant should give the same recommendation regardless of whether a user's name sounds male or female. How should a tester design this check?

options.A: Run the same scenario with only the name varied across a set of names associated with different genders, and assert the substantive recommendation does not change
options.B: Run the scenario once with a randomly chosen name, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.C: Only test with a single gender-neutral name, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play
options.D: Skip this check since names should not affect output by default, which might seem reasonable on the surface but is contradicted by how these systems are actually built and tested

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: run the same scenario with only the name varied across a set of names associated with different genders, and assert the substantive recommendation does not change.

questions.question: A tester wants to validate that an assistant's confidence language matches its accuracy, so it should hedge on uncertain answers, not just on easy ones. What test design checks this?

options.B: Compare the assistant's hedging and confidence language against measured correctness across a set of questions spanning easy to genuinely uncertain topics
options.A: Only test with questions the assistant is certain to answer correctly, though closer inspection of the system's behaviour shows this is not the case
options.C: Assert the assistant never hedges on any question, which sounds plausible but is not supported by how the underlying mechanism works
options.D: Assert the assistant always hedges on every question, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: compare the assistant's hedging and confidence language against measured correctness across a set of questions spanning easy to genuinely uncertain topics.

questions.question: A team compares two RAG configurations using only end-to-end answer correctness. Reviewers cannot tell whether gains come from retrieval or generation. What should the evaluation add?

options.A: Separate retrieval metrics, such as recall at k, alongside generation and answer-correctness metrics
options.B: Nothing; end-to-end correctness alone is always sufficient, which testers often assume
options.C: Remove retrieval metrics entirely to simplify reporting, which confuses two separate concepts
options.D: Replace all metrics with latency only, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: separate retrieval metrics, such as recall at k, alongside generation and answer-correctness metrics, so each pipeline stage's contribution is visible.

questions.question: A team's human evaluators are shown which model produced each response before scoring. Scores consistently favour the team's own model. What evaluation flaw does this suggest, and how should it be fixed?

options.B: Evaluator bias from knowing the source
options.A: The evaluators need more training on grammar rules
options.C: The rubric has too many criteria
options.D: The sample size is too large

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: evaluator bias from knowing the source; fix by blinding evaluators to which system produced each response.

questions.question: An LLM-judge is asked to score responses from 1 to 10 but nearly all scores cluster between 7 and 8, making comparisons hard to interpret. What change would likely help?

options.C: Switch to pairwise comparisons, or a rubric with clearer, more distinct level definitions
options.A: Widen the scale to 1 to 1000, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: Ask the judge to always give a 10, which confuses two separate concepts
options.D: Remove the judge and use no evaluation at all, which is a frequent misreading

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: switch to pairwise comparisons, or a rubric with clearer, more distinct level definitions, so the judge can differentiate quality more effectively.

questions.question: A team wants to validate a new automated groundedness metric before relying on it. What is the correct validation approach?

options.C: Compare the metric's scores against human-labelled groundedness judgements on a representative sample and measure agreement before trusting it for gating
options.A: Assume the metric is valid because it is popular in a published paper, though closer inspection of the system's behaviour shows this is not the case
options.B: Skip validation and use it directly for release gates, which might seem reasonable on the surface but is contradicted by how these systems are actually built and tested
options.D: Validate it only once, using the same data it was built to evaluate, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: compare the metric's scores against human-labelled groundedness judgements on a representative sample and measure agreement before trusting it for gating.

questions.question: A code-generation evaluation reports 85% pass at 1 but the team wants a realistic estimate of user-facing success when the assistant is allowed to retry. Which metric better answers that question?

options.A: Pass at k for a k matching the number of retries actually available to the user
options.B: BLEU score against a single reference solution, which is a frequent misreading
options.C: Average token length of generated code, which confuses two separate concepts
options.D: Response latency percentile, though it misses the actual cause

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: pass at k for a k matching the number of retries actually available to the user.

questions.question: A team measures human-eval win-rate for a new prompt using only 15 comparisons and gets 73% in favour. What should the tester recommend before declaring victory?

options.A: Increase the sample size
options.B: Declare the result final since 73% is well above 50%
options.C: Reduce the sample size further to save cost
options.D: Switch immediately to production without further evaluation

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: increase the sample size, since 15 comparisons give a wide confidence interval and the result may not be statistically meaningful.

questions.question: A team evaluates a chatbot's helpfulness only on questions it answered without refusing. What bias does this introduce?

options.B: Survivorship bias
options.A: No bias; excluding refusals is standard best practice
options.C: A latency bias only
options.D: A licensing bias only

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: survivorship bias; excluding refused or failed cases inflates the apparent helpfulness score by ignoring where the system did not even attempt to help.

questions.question: A dataset used to evaluate a summarisation model's factuality has only easy, short documents. The tool then scores very high. What should the tester conclude?

options.C: The score likely overstates real-world performance
options.A: The score can be trusted as representative of all use cases
options.B: Short documents are always representative of real content
options.D: The metric itself must be broken, though this is not accurate

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: the score likely overstates real-world performance; the evaluation set needs harder and longer documents representative of production use.

questions.question: Two teams report different faithfulness scores for the same model because one used an NLI-based automated check and the other used human review. How should this discrepancy be handled?

options.C: Investigate where the two methods disagree, treat the human-reviewed result as more authoritative, and calibrate or document the automated metric's error pattern
options.A: Average the two scores without further investigation, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review

questions.question: A GenAI writing tool sometimes reproduces distinctive phrases from a specific living author's copyrighted work. What test and governance response is appropriate?

questions.question: An incident review finds that a GenAI feature exposed one customer's order details to a different logged-in customer due to a session-handling bug interacting with the retrieval step. What test category should have caught this before release?
